name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Confident and Wrong: The Dunning-Kruger Effect in Crypto Discourse
lesson.summary: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with limited knowledge in a domain tend to overestimate their own competence, a pattern that plays out loudly wherever blockchain technology is discussed with confidence but little underlying expertise.
lesson.body:
The Dunning-Kruger effect comes from a 1999 study by Justin Kruger and David Dunning, who tested participants on skills such as logical reasoning, grammar, and humor, then asked each participant to estimate how their performance ranked against their peers. People who scored in the bottom quartile on the actual tests substantially overestimated their own percentile, often placing themselves near the middle of the pack, while the highest performers were slightly more accurate, and on some measures mildly underestimated their own relative standing. The core finding is about calibration within a specific domain: the same skills required to perform well at a task are often the skills required to judge performance at that task accurately, so a lack of competence can hide itself from the person who has it.

The effect is frequently overstated in popular discussion. It does not claim that unskilled people believe themselves to be geniuses, or that every novice is wildly overconfident about everything, and it is not a general claim that expertise makes people humble across the board. It is a narrower, domain specific finding about the correlation between low competence and inflated self assessment relative to actual peers on a defined task, and the gap shrinks, rather than disappears entirely, as real skill increases.

Blockchain discourse offers a near constant supply of this pattern. Someone who has read a handful of social media threads and a project's marketing page can produce a fully confident explanation of how a new consensus mechanism works, how it is mathematically superior to established alternatives, or why a particular token is destined to replace a national currency, often with more certainty than the cryptographers and distributed systems researchers who actually built the underlying protocols express about their own work. Genuine experts in consensus algorithms or applied cryptography tend to hedge, citing open problems, known attack vectors, and unresolved trade offs, precisely because enough domain knowledge to see the difficulty of the problem tends to produce more caution, not less.

This matters for evaluating blockchain claims because confidence is a poor proxy for accuracy in any technical field with a steep learning curve, and cryptography, distributed consensus, and mechanism design all qualify. A speaker's certainty, fluency of jargon, or willingness to make sweeping predictions says very little about whether their underlying claims are correct. If anything, in a field this technical, a source who acknowledges specific limitations, uncertainties, or open research questions is often demonstrating more actual competence than one who has a confident answer for every question.

The practical response is twofold. When evaluating someone else's blockchain claims, weight demonstrated track record, specific technical detail, and acknowledged uncertainty more heavily than confidence or jargon. And when evaluating your own understanding, especially after a few hours of reading about a new protocol, it is worth explicitly asking whether that reading has produced real competence or just enough vocabulary to sound competent, since the Dunning-Kruger effect applies to the skeptical reader exactly as much as it applies to the enthusiastic promoter.
